paragraphs: This paper describes a chip that classifies and supports compression of electrical signals recorded inside the heart. Its inputs are analogue vectors with 30 components. Vector quantization represents these inputs through matching templates, connecting the task of recognizing signal patterns with the task of describing them using a compact representation.

The central design feature is adaptive template matching that tolerates changes in amplitude and timing. Timing tolerance includes shifts between samples and shifts within a sampling interval. This matters because a signal can change in strength or alignment while retaining the shape that makes it relevant to classification. The matching procedure accommodates those variations.

The authors report operation at a maximum power consumption of 2.5 microwatts from a 3.3-volt supply when processing one vector per second, corresponding to 60 heartbeats per minute. They emphasize unsupervised classification of abnormal rhythms and computational support for low-bit-rate compression. The contribution combines these capabilities with a measured low-power hardware implementation.
neurips-1998-a-micropower-cmos-adaptive-.tldr: An adaptive analogue chip classifies and supports compression of heart signals while tolerating amplitude and timing changes at very low power.

paragraphs: This paper presents a sound localization system that uses a single microphone. Its biological inspiration is the human ability to estimate a sound source's elevation with one ear. The outer ear changes incoming sound through reflections and diffraction, making its physical shape part of the process that supplies information about source location.

The proposed system gives the microphone a specially shaped reflecting structure that serves a similar role. Analogue circuitry then processes echo timing to localize the sound. The approach links physical acoustics with computation: the reflecting structure creates useful timing information, and the electronics interpret that information. Both parts contribute to obtaining location cues from one microphone.

The authors designed and fabricated a CMOS integrated circuit and report a successful demonstration using actual sounds. This establishes a hardware realization of the proposed localization mechanism. The stated contribution is a working combination of an ear-inspired acoustic structure and dedicated analogue processing, showing how a single acoustic sensor can support sound localization.
neurips-1998-a-neuromorphic-monaural-sou.tldr: An ear-inspired reflecting structure and analogue echo-timing circuit enable sound localization with a single microphone.

paragraphs: This paper develops an analogue neural chip set for active noise cancellation. Learning takes place on the chips themselves through an implementation of error backpropagation. The hardware therefore combines signal processing with the ability to adapt its behavior, making learning part of the operating noise-cancellation system rather than a separate preparation step.

The chips have a modular design, with direct pin connections that allow them to be combined on boards. Their adaptive circuits compensate for several complications in acoustic cancellation: sound traveling through multiple paths, random noise, and nonlinear loudspeaker distortion. These effects matter because the acoustic channel and the loudspeaker both influence the sound that the system must cancel.

The assembled neural board demonstrated active cancellation without a digital signal processor, and the authors report experiments canceling car noise in real time. The finding ties the learning circuitry to a practical acoustic task. It shows that the proposed analogue hardware can perform adaptive cancellation while directly accommodating the stated channel and loudspeaker effects.
neurips-1998-active-noise-canceling-usin.tldr: Analogue neural chips with onboard backpropagation learning demonstrate real-time car-noise cancellation without a digital signal processor.

paragraphs: This paper uses a quantitative model of early vision to explain how attention changes people's ability to distinguish visual patterns. The model combines visual filters that interact nonlinearly with a statistically efficient decision process. Its target is discrimination thresholds: the levels at which differences between patterns become distinguishable in the tested tasks.

The authors automatically fit the model to observations from four classical discrimination tasks performed while another task occupied attention. A single modeling framework reproduces the thresholds across all four tasks simultaneously. This gives the analysis a shared starting point for examining what changes when attention becomes fully available for visual discrimination.

The model then attributes the observed, seemingly complicated improvements in certain thresholds to stronger competition among early visual filters. This matters because several behavioral changes can be interpreted through a common adjustment to the interactions within the model. The result is a model-based explanation of attention's effects, with strengthened filter competition identified as the best explanation within the reported analysis.
neurips-1998-attentional-modulation-of-h.tldr: A quantitative vision model explains attention-related improvements in pattern discrimination through stronger competition among early visual filters.

paragraphs: This paper develops a faster way to compute convolution, an operation widely used in signal processing and pattern recognition. Its motivation is that feature extraction often deals with signals whose relevant features are already distorted. In such settings, accepting some approximation can be worthwhile when it substantially reduces the computation needed to extract those features.

The method first approximates regions of a signal with low-degree polynomials. It then differentiates this representation until the resulting signal consists of impulses or their derivatives. Convolution becomes particularly simple in that form. Integrating the convolution result reverses the differentiation step, recovering the corresponding convolution while retaining the initial signal approximation.

The authors report substantial acceleration in feature extraction and identify convolutional neural networks as an application. The key idea is to change the representation in which convolution is performed so that the expensive operation becomes simpler. Its practical justification is the stated tradeoff between computational accuracy and speed in applications where precise reproduction of an already distorted signal is less important.
neurips-1998-boxlets-a-fast-convolution-.tldr: Boxlets accelerate convolution by approximating signals with polynomials, differentiating them into impulses, and integrating the simplified convolution result.

paragraphs: This paper treats finding visual contours in clutter as a Bayesian inference problem. It defines a probabilistic collection of search problems and evaluates candidate contours using a global criterion that combines local image intensity with geometry. This connects evidence at individual image locations with the overall shape of the contour being sought.

The authors analyze how quickly A* search algorithms converge on these problems. They use information theory to bound the probability of rare events within the defined collection of instances. The analysis identifies characteristics of the problem domain, called order parameters, that determine convergence rates. Search efficiency is thereby connected to properties of the visual evidence and problem distribution.

For a particular admissible A* algorithm with pruning, the authors report high-probability convergence with expected running time linear in problem size. This is a probabilistic result within their framework, rather than an unconditional statement about every image. They also outline extensions concerning fundamental contour detectability and search using non-admissible heuristics, connecting computational efficiency with the availability of enough evidence to detect a contour.
neurips-1998-convergence-rates-of-algori.tldr: A Bayesian analysis identifies conditions under which a pruned A* contour-search algorithm has linear expected running time.

paragraphs: Reaching to grasp an object requires relating its visually observed position to the arm's joint angles. This is an inverse kinematics problem: a desired hand location must be translated into the coordinates that describe the arm's configuration. The paper focuses on learning the hand-position feedback controller involved in solving that transformation.

The proposed model uses two linked changes: a change in the joint-angle vector and the corresponding change in the squared magnitude of the hand-position error. The latter measures how far the hand is from its target. Relating these quantities gives the learning process information about how a joint movement changes the size of the positioning error.

This approach matters because it places changes in task error at the center of learning the visual feedback transformation. The learning signal connects movement in joint coordinates with progress toward the visible target. Numerical simulations illustrate the model's feasibility, supporting the claim that the proposed relationship can be used to learn the controller within the simulated setting.
neurips-1998-coordinate-transformation-l.tldr: A simulated hand-position controller learns coordinate transformations by relating joint movements to changes in squared positioning error.

paragraphs: This paper introduces Direct Optimization Of Margins, abbreviated DOOM, in the setting of combined classifiers. The supplied evidence compares DOOM with AdaBoost using cumulative distributions of training margins. That comparison makes the distribution of margins central to understanding how the two methods behave on their training examples.

The reported result is a tradeoff: DOOM accepts a substantial increase in training error while obtaining lower test error. These two measurements describe performance on different sets of examples. The observation therefore shows that, in the presented comparison, improving the fit to the training examples is not the same as improving performance on test examples.

The title frames direct margin optimization as a way to improve generalization, and the supplied comparison supports that framing through the reported test-error improvement. Its substantive message is that a combined classifier can benefit from an optimization choice even when that choice worsens training error. The margin distributions provide the accompanying view of training behavior, while the test-error comparison supplies the stated evidence of better generalization.
neurips-1998-direct-optimization-of-marg.tldr: DOOM directly optimizes classifier margins and reports lower test error than AdaBoost despite substantially higher training error.

paragraphs: This paper studies reinforcement learning when an agent's current observation does not fully describe its environment. Under partial observability, methods such as Q-learning may lose their effectiveness. Maintaining memory and estimating the hidden state can address that difficulty, but the authors identify the computational cost of such approaches as a motivation for another strategy.

The strategy is a stochastic memoryless policy. For each current observation, it assigns probabilities to the available actions without consulting a history of observations. The objective is to maximize average reward per time step. Randomized action selection therefore becomes part of the policy itself, while the representation avoids the expense of maintaining a state estimate.

The authors present a variation of an existing algorithm for learning a locally optimal policy of this kind, discuss implementation, and demonstrate viability on four test problems. The contribution supplies empirical support for an approach that had previously been proposed without empirical verification. Its stated target remains local optimality within the class of stochastic memoryless policies.
neurips-1998-experimental-results-on-lea.tldr: Experiments support learning randomized, memoryless action policies as a practical approach to partially observable reinforcement learning.

paragraphs: This paper examines a neural network called ARTMAP-FD on radar pulse data collected in the field. The network performs two related tasks. Identification assigns a test pattern to a class encountered during training. Familiarity discrimination asks whether the pattern belongs to any of the classes represented in that training experience.

The distinction changes what a successful recognition system must decide. Naming a familiar class addresses which known category fits a pattern; judging familiarity addresses whether the known categories cover it at all. By including both tasks, the paper treats recognition as involving both a class assignment and a judgment about the applicability of the learned class set.

The evaluation compares ARTMAP-FD with NEN, a nearest-neighbor-based algorithm, and with an extension of NEN that uses a value of k greater than one. The stated contribution is an empirical examination of these methods on field radar data. The supplied abstract establishes the tasks and comparison being studied, without specifying a winning method or a numerical performance outcome.
neurips-1998-familiarity-discrimination-.tldr: ARTMAP-FD is evaluated on field radar pulses for both class identification and deciding whether a pulse belongs to any learned class.

paragraphs: Learning a nonlinear state-space model requires reasoning about hidden states from observed data. This paper develops Monte Carlo generalized EM equations for that task. The main difficulty is the expectation step, which requires samples from the posterior distribution of hidden states: the distribution describing which states remain plausible after observing the data.

The authors make sampling easier by approximating that posterior with a Gaussian distribution. They obtain its parameters using either an extended Kalman filter or Fisher scoring. Independent samples are then straightforward to generate from the approximation. When the posterior has several distinct peaks, they use a mixture of Gaussians so that the approximation can represent multiple plausible explanations.

The reported experiments favor sampling from these approximate posteriors over using single hidden-state estimates. Fisher scoring also approximates the posterior mode better than the extended Kalman filter in the reported experiment, while the mixture approach performs better for a multimodal distribution. Together, these findings support retaining uncertainty and, when necessary, multiple modes during learning.
neurips-1998-fisher-scoring-and-a-mixtur.tldr: Sampling Gaussian or Gaussian-mixture approximations of hidden-state uncertainty improves nonlinear state-space learning over single-state estimates.

paragraphs: This paper asks how kernel principal component analysis can support reconstruction and noise removal, extending uses familiar from ordinary PCA. Linear PCA represents data along directions ordered by their variance, allowing selected directions to be retained. Kernel PCA offers nonlinear features, but using those features to produce reconstructed inputs introduces an additional problem.

The difficulty is that kernel PCA's outputs live in a high-dimensional feature space. A point obtained there need not correspond exactly to any possible input. Consequently, computing a useful feature representation does not automatically provide a way to turn that representation back into a reconstructed data point. This is the pre-image problem addressed by the paper.

The authors propose ways to find approximate pre-images, concentrating on Gaussian kernels. They demonstrate reconstruction and denoising with those approximations on both toy examples and real-world data. The contribution connects nonlinear feature extraction to outputs in the original input space, making it possible to use the learned features for recovering data as well as preparing it for classification.
neurips-1998-kernel-pca-and-de-noising-i.tldr: Approximate pre-images let kernel PCA turn nonlinear feature representations back into reconstructed and denoised data.

paragraphs: This paper addresses visual invariance: recognizing an object as the same despite transformations such as movement, rotation, or scaling. It proposes a Bayesian learning method based on Lie groups. The mathematical framework describes transformations in a way that can connect small changes in an image with larger transformations of that image.

The authors use an image-generating model based on a matrix exponential and derive an online, unsupervised algorithm for learning transformation operators. Training data contain infinitesimal transformations, and learning maximizes the posterior probability of generating those data. The approach includes earlier first-order Taylor approximations as special cases while being capable, in principle, of representing arbitrarily large transformations.

Experiments suggest that the method can learn operators handling reasonably large one-dimensional translations and two-dimensional rotations. This distinction between theoretical scope and demonstrated behavior matters: the framework supports large transformations in principle, while the evidence concerns those specific transformation types. The central contribution is learning a transformation structure from small changes that remains useful for larger changes.
neurips-1998-learning-lie-groups-for-inv.tldr: A Bayesian Lie-group model learns visual transformation operators from tiny changes and demonstrates handling larger translations and rotations.

paragraphs: This paper extends expectation-maximization to learning nonlinear dynamical systems whose internal states cannot be observed directly. The learning problem has two connected unknowns: the sequence of hidden states and the parameters governing the system. EM addresses them iteratively, using the current model to estimate hidden states and then using those estimates to revise the model.

The expectation step uses extended Kalman smoothing to estimate the hidden states. The maximization step updates the parameters while accounting for uncertainty in those state estimates. This uncertainty is central to the computational difficulty: nonlinear parameter updates generally require integrating over possible states, rather than simply treating an estimated trajectory as known.

The authors show that choosing Gaussian radial basis functions to represent the nonlinear relationships makes the required integrals tractable. With that representation, the maximization step reduces to solving systems of linear equations. The contribution is therefore a combination of approximate state inference and a carefully chosen nonlinear model that makes uncertainty-aware parameter learning computationally manageable.
neurips-1998-learning-nonlinear-dynamica.tldr: An EM method combines extended Kalman smoothing with Gaussian radial basis functions to make nonlinear dynamical-system parameter updates tractable.

paragraphs: This paper tackles finding people in images by assembling candidate body segments. People are difficult objects to recognize because their articulated bodies can take different configurations. The method uses constraints arising from the body's kinematic properties to decide which collections of possible segments are consistent with the appearance of a person.

The computational obstacle is the number of combinations. The authors state that a reasonable person model needs at least nine segments, making it impractical to submit every possible group to a classifier. They prune the search using projected versions of a classifier designed to accept complete groups corresponding to people. This lets classifier information guide the search before every assembly is fully considered.

The paper describes an efficient projection algorithm for a popular classifier and demonstrates detection of whether real-scene images contain people. Its contribution links a structured body representation with a way to manage the resulting combinatorial search. The recognition constraints help determine both what counts as a plausible person and which candidate assemblies deserve further consideration.
neurips-1998-learning-to-find-pictures-o.tldr: A person-detection method assembles plausible body segments and uses projected classifiers to prune the otherwise overwhelming search.

paragraphs: This paper connects the statistics of natural monochrome images with response suppression in primary visual cortex. The authors decompose images using wavelets at multiple scales. Although the resulting coefficients have little ordinary correlation, their rectified values remain strongly related across nearby positions, orientations, and scales. These higher-order dependencies survive purely linear processing.

The proposed statistical remedy is divisive normalization: divide each coefficient by a weighted combination of rectified neighboring coefficients. Similar computations already appear in models of visual neurons. The analysis gives those computations a statistical rationale and, more specifically, uses measured image dependencies to determine the weights contributing to the normalization signal.

The derived weighting is qualitatively consistent with physiological experiments showing that stimuli outside a neuron's classical receptive field can suppress its response. This links a property of natural images to a property of neural processing. The result supports the hypothesis that early vision is adapted to image statistics, with surrounding activity providing information relevant to normalizing a local response.
neurips-1998-modeling-surround-suppressi.tldr: Natural-image statistics determine divisive-normalization weights that qualitatively match observed surround suppression in visual cortex.

paragraphs: This paper proposes identifying neuronal spikes in multi-electrode recordings through relationships between recording channels. It assumes a stable linear relationship between each cell and each electrode, determined by tissue properties, electrode properties, and their relative geometry. These relationships are described by transfer functions, and the method works with ratios of those functions.

The stated advantage is insensitivity to changes in a spike's shape or amplitude. The method bases sorting on the relationships across electrodes, allowing those relationships to identify spike types even when individual waveforms vary. The stability and linearity assumptions are essential because they make the transfer-function relationships a dependable basis for grouping events.

Processing has two stages. First, the algorithm clusters transfer-function ratios to build templates describing the statistics of each spike type. It then detects spikes in the recordings using those statistics. The authors apply the techniques to data from the cockroach escape-response system, demonstrating the proposed workflow on a biological recording application.
neurips-1998-multi-electrode-spike-sorti.tldr: Clustering transfer-function ratios across electrodes sorts neuronal spikes while tolerating waveform and amplitude variation under a stable linear recording model.

paragraphs: This paper proposes a modular account of how people learn and select movements under different environmental conditions. The architecture contains multiple pairs of models. Within each pair, an inverse model acts as a controller, while a forward model acts as a predictor. Together, the pairs provide multiple ways to control movement and anticipate its consequences.

The architecture learns both the inverse models needed for control and how to select models appropriate to the current environment. This couples acquiring motor skills with deciding when to use them. That combination matters when the same person must manipulate different objects and the correct control behavior depends on which object or conditions are currently encountered.

Object-manipulation simulations demonstrate learning for multiple objects and appropriate generalization to new ones. They also reproduce a feature of the size-weight illusion: visual cues initially activate an inappropriate motor program, followed by correction during the action. The results connect successful adaptation and a characteristic initial error to the same modular learning-and-selection architecture.
neurips-1998-multiple-paired-forward-inv.tldr: Paired prediction and control models learn object-specific motor behavior, select suitable controllers, and reproduce correction in the size-weight illusion.

paragraphs: This paper develops a probabilistic account of illusory contours, the boundaries perceived between supplied visual cues. It builds on a model in which candidate shapes are traced by particles moving at constant speed while their directions change according to Brownian motion. Such a construction describes a distribution of possible contours rather than selecting a single connecting curve.

The earlier model takes constraints specifying both position and direction, then produces contours joining pairs of constraints. Two shortcomings motivate the new work: those contours generally remain open, and their distribution depends on scale. This leaves closure and consistent treatment across sizes unresolved within that formulation.

The authors show how to compute a scale-invariant distribution of closed contours using position constraints alone. Closing the contours makes complete boundaries part of the construction, while removing explicit directional inputs reduces what must be specified beforehand. They use the resulting distribution to explain a known illusory-contour effect, linking the mathematical treatment of contour shape to a perceptual phenomenon.
neurips-1998-orientation-scale-and-disco.tldr: A probabilistic contour model derives closed, scale-invariant boundaries from position cues alone and explains an illusory-contour effect.

paragraphs: This paper studies classification of faces into five orientations when labeled images are scarce. It compares three probabilistic models with different treatments of pixel relationships. One treats pixels independently, another permits a set of arbitrary pairwise dependencies, and the third restricts dependencies to neighboring pixels. This makes the use of unlabeled data testable across different model structures.

The authors use expectation-maximization to combine a small labeled training set with a much larger unlabeled set. The motivation is practical: assigning image labels can be difficult, while unlabeled images are readily available. The experiments show that adding unlabeled images can substantially improve accuracy for all three model types.

The abstract reports 94% accuracy with two randomly selected labeled examples per class and 98% in a setting described as using six labeled examples. These findings demonstrate that useful orientation classification can be learned with very little labeling in the reported task. The broader contribution is evidence that unlabeled images can benefit models with several different assumptions about pixel dependencies.
neurips-1998-probabilistic-modeling-for-.tldr: Using EM to add unlabeled images greatly improves five-way face-orientation classification when labeled examples are scarce.

paragraphs: This paper approaches graph isomorphism through an equivalent maximum-clique problem. Graph isomorphism concerns whether two graphs have the same structure under a correspondence between their vertices. The reformulation turns that structural matching task into the search for a largest collection of mutually connected vertices in the associated clique formulation.

A mathematical result connecting maximum cliques with quadratic optimization provides the next step. The authors express the problem as a standard quadratic program and use replicator equations to optimize it. These equations are simple dynamical systems originating in theoretical biology, available in both continuous-time and discrete-time forms. They supply the mechanism for moving toward a solution.

The experiments produce results competitive with more elaborate mean-field annealing heuristics. The authors explicitly acknowledge that the replicator dynamics cannot escape local solutions, so the approach retains that limitation. Its significance is that a relatively simple dynamical optimization procedure performs competitively in the reported tests despite this restriction, providing a practical energy-minimization framework for the graph problem.
neurips-1998-replicator-equations-maxima.tldr: Replicator dynamics solve a quadratic reformulation of graph isomorphism competitively with more elaborate heuristics despite getting trapped in local solutions.

paragraphs: This paper analyzes how neuronal noise reduces the information carried by a synaptic signal as it travels along a dendrite. The dendrite is modeled as an infinite linear cable with noise distributed along its length. This idealized representation lets the authors derive analytical measures of signal degradation during electrical propagation.

The analysis includes thermal noise, noise from the random behavior of voltage-dependent potassium and sodium channels, and synaptic noise from spontaneous background activity. Information transfer is framed as a detection task: determine whether a presynaptic spike occurred by observing the postsynaptic membrane voltage. This turns signal reliability into a concrete question about distinguishing spike presence from absence.

Under the chosen parameters, spontaneous synaptic activity is the dominant source of noise and limits the distance over which information can be transmitted reliably. The parameter qualification is part of the finding. The contribution is a common analytical framework for comparing the noise sources and identifying which one constrains detection in the modeled setting.
neurips-1998-signal-detection-in-noisy-w.tldr: An analytical dendrite model finds that background synaptic noise dominates the limit on reliable spike detection for the parameters studied.

paragraphs: This paper addresses a local-optimum problem in fitting finite mixture models with expectation-maximization. A mixture represents data using several components, but learning can allocate those components poorly. The authors highlight configurations with too many components covering one region and too few covering another region far away.

Their split-and-merge EM algorithm repeatedly performs paired restructuring operations. Splitting a component provides more modeling capacity in one place, while merging components frees capacity elsewhere. A new selection criterion identifies promising split and merge candidates efficiently. The operations are intended to escape configurations that ordinary parameter adjustment has left at a poor local maximum.

The authors apply the method to Gaussian mixtures and mixtures of factor analyzers on synthetic and real data. They report improvements in likelihood for both training data and held-out test data. The training result indicates better fitting of the observed examples, while the held-out result shows that the benefit also extends to examples outside the fitting set in the reported experiments.
neurips-1998-smem-algorithm-for-mixture-.tldr: Split-and-merge EM reallocates mixture components to escape poor local optima and improves training and held-out likelihoods.

paragraphs: This paper develops approximations for probabilistic graphical models, whose computations can become prohibitively expensive as graphs grow. Variational methods address this by replacing a difficult distribution with a more manageable one. The paper focuses on enriching that substitute distribution beyond the standard factorized approach, which represents variables without retaining their dependencies.

The authors introduce two tractable families: decimatable Boltzmann machines and tractable belief networks. These provide undirected and directed approximation structures, respectively. They derive generalized mean-field equations for both families, giving procedures for using the richer structures within the variational framework. The aim is to preserve useful relationships while keeping the approximation computationally accessible.

Simulations on a small benchmark suggest favorable performance compared with previously reported alternatives. That result supports the value of retaining more structure in an approximation, within the scope of the reported problem. The contribution combines a choice of manageable distribution families with the equations needed to use them, expanding the available options between fully factorized approximations and the original difficult model.
neurips-1998-tractable-variational-struc.tldr: Two structured variational families retain dependencies beyond factorized approximations while allowing tractable graphical-model computations.

paragraphs: This paper tackles the difficulty of interpreting probabilistic clustering results in high-dimensional or abstract data spaces. Cluster assignments can express uncertainty and relationships between groups, but a collection of assignment probabilities is difficult to understand by inspection. The goal is to turn that information into a low-dimensional picture of the data's group structure.

The method builds a statistical model of object assignments that have been observed or estimated by a probabilistic clustering procedure. It embeds objects in a low-dimensional Euclidean space by using a Gaussian mixture model to approximate the observed statistics. The visualization is therefore organized around the probabilistic grouping information supplied to the method.

This design allows the approach to accommodate varied data types, including histograms, proximities, and co-occurrences. The authors demonstrate it by visualizing histograms of textured images in a large-scale data-mining application. The contribution is a way to make clustering relationships visually accessible when the original data representation or its assignment variables are difficult to interpret directly.
neurips-1998-visualizing-group-structure.tldr: A Gaussian-mixture embedding turns probabilistic cluster assignments into low-dimensional visualizations of group structure across varied data types.
